title: Question 8
stem:
An incomplete circuit diagram of a bridge rectifier is shown in Fig. 8.1.

{{figure:figure_8_1}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Complete Fig. 8.1 for the bridge rectifier such that the point A is at a positive potential with respect to point B.

markscheme_points.text: four diodes shown (one in each gap) with correct circuit symbols
all four diodes connected in correct direction (pointing left to right)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what a diode does - it only lets conventional current pass one way. For point A to stay positive, current must always enter the load at A and leave at B, no matter which way the a.c. supply is pushing.

Hint 2: Identify the two output nodes: D connects to A (needs to be positive) and C connects to B (needs to be negative). Work out which way current must flow through each of the four gaps to always flow into D and out of C.
parts.proper_answer: Insert four diode symbols in the four gaps with forward direction pointing from left to right, i.e. towards D and away from C, so that D (A) is always positive with respect to C (B).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall how the bridge steers current**
You have four gaps forming a diamond between the a.c. input (top and bottom wires) and the d.c. output (C on the left, D on the right). A diode triangle points in the direction of allowed conventional current, bar is the blocking end.

Step 2: **Force A positive**
A is wired to D and B is wired to C. So D must always be the positive output. That means current must always flow *into* D from the bridge and *out of* C back to the bridge, on both half-cycles of the a.c. This happens if all diodes point left to right: top-wire to D, C to top-wire, bottom-wire to D, C to bottom-wire. Draw the four correct diode symbols in those orientations.

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 8.2, draw a line to show the variation of the potential difference $V$ across the load resistor with time $t$. Your line should extend from $t = 0.5T$ to $t = 2.0T$.

markscheme_points.text: three lines showing exponential decay from the peaks at 0.5T, 1.0T and 1.5T, ending at the point where the decay meets the next rising peak
three curved lines rising along the upwards dotted lines from the minima to the peaks at 1.0T, 1.5T and 2.0T

hints: Hint 1: Remember what the capacitor does without drawing yet - it charges up quickly to the peak $V_0$ when the rectified p.d. rises, then discharges slowly through the load when the rectified p.d. falls.
Hint 2: Use the ripple information - maximum minus minimum is $33\%$ of $V_0$. Work out what fraction of $V_0$ the minimum level must sit at on the $V$-axis.

Hint 3: Think about the shape of the two parts of each cycle - the falling part is a slow exponential discharge starting at each peak, and the rising part is a quick recharge that follows the dotted rectified curve back up to the next peak.
parts.proper_answer: From $t = 0.5T$ to $2.0T$: exponential decay curves starting at each peak $V_0$, falling to a minimum of $(1-0.33)V_0 = 0.67V_0$, then rising sharply along the dotted curve to the next peak. Three such saw-tooth-like ripples shown.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the ripple minimum level**
The capacitor charges to the peak $V_0$. It then discharges a little before the next peak recharges it. Ripple = $V_{max} - V_{min} = 0.33V_0$. So: $$V_{min} = V_0 - 0.33V_0 = 0.67V_0 = \frac{2}{3}V_0$$ Mark this level - about two-thirds up the $V$-axis.

Step 2: **Draw the discharge - slow fall**
Starting at each peak at $0.5T$, $1.0T$, $1.5T$, draw a slightly curved exponential fall. It does not fall to zero, it only falls to $\frac{2}{3}V_0$ where it meets the next rising dotted line.

Step 3: **Draw the charge - fast rise**
From each minimum, draw a short rising curve that follows up the dotted full-wave rectified curve to the next peak at $1.0T$, $1.5T$, $2.0T$. Repeat for three cycles between $0.5T$ and $2.0T$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use your line in (b)(i) to determine, in terms of $T$, the time constant of the smoothing circuit.

markscheme_points.text: from graph: discharge time (from V0 to (2/3)V0) = (11/30) T

hints: Hint 1: The falling part of your smoothed curve is a capacitor discharging through the resistor. Focus on one discharge - it starts at $V_0$ at a peak and ends at $(2/3)V_0$ just before the next peak. Estimate that time interval from the $t$-axis in terms of $T$.
Hint 2: Recall how discharging voltage depends on time and time constant - the voltage starts at $V_0$ and decays exponentially while the capacitor is isolated from the supply.
Hint 3: Take natural logs of both sides to isolate the time constant $\tau$. Check that your discharge time from the graph is about $0.37T$ and solve for $\tau$ in terms of $T$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the discharge time from your line**
Take one cycle, e.g. peak at $1.0T$ falling to minimum just before $1.5T$. Measuring on Fig. 8.2, the fall from $V_0$ to $\frac{2}{3}V_0$ lasts: $$t_d = \frac{11}{30}T \approx 0.37T$$ This is less than $0.5T$ because the capacitor recharges before the rectified voltage reaches zero.

Step 2: **Apply the discharge equation**
While discharging, the p.d. follows: $$V = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau}\right)$$ At $t = t_d$, $V = \frac{2}{3}V_0$: $$\frac{2}{3}V_0 = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t_d}{\tau}\right)$$

Step 3: **Solve for the time constant**
Cancel $V_0$ and take ln: $$\ln\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = -\frac{t_d}{\tau}$$ $$\tau = -\frac{t_d}{\ln(2/3)} = \frac{11T/30}{0.405} \approx 0.90T$$ So time constant $= 0.90T$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The resistance of the load resistor is now increased. The capacitance of the capacitor is unchanged.

State and explain the effect of this change on the smoothed output p.d.

markscheme_points.text:
line shows a larger minimum voltage
or
smaller difference between maximum and minimum voltages

hints: Hint 1: Start from what controls how fast the capacitor loses voltage between peaks - think about what $\tau = RC$ tells you when $R$ gets larger but $C$ stays the same.
Hint 2: If the discharge is slower, what does that mean for how far the voltage can fall before the next peak tops it up again, and how does that change the shape you drew in (b)(i)?
parts.proper_answer: Time constant $\tau = RC$ increases. Capacitor discharges more slowly, so minimum voltage is higher and ripple (difference between max and min) is smaller - output is more smoothly d.c.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link resistance to time constant**
For the smoothing circuit: $$\tau = RC$$ $C$ is unchanged but $R$ is increased, so $\tau$ increases. A larger time constant means slower exponential discharge.

Step 2: **Explain the effect on the output**
Between peaks there is less time for charge to leak through the larger resistor, so $V$ falls less far from $V_0$. The minimum rises, the max-min difference shrinks, giving better smoothing, closer to pure d.c.
